title: Coming to the Guru
hook: before a call that matters, you sit up. before the Guru's words, hands are washed and heads covered
tomorrow: what's the little book wrapped in cloth on the high shelf?

segments.voice: Year four closed on a promise: next, the granth itself. Here it is. And the first question isn't how to read it. It's how to come to it.
screen: `NEXT, THE GRANTH ITSELF.` → `HOW DO YOU COME TO IT?`

segments.voice: Before a video call that matters, people do small things nobody asked for. Close the other tabs. Check their hair. Sit up. Nobody grades it; it's just how a body says, this one counts. In Sikh homes and gurdwaras there's an older version of that. Before the Guru's words are opened, on paper or on a screen, hands get washed and heads get covered. So, one question for the first day of the year: why wash your hands to read?
screen: `CLOSE THE TABS. SIT UP.` → `HANDS WASHED, HEAD COVERED.` → `WHY WASH YOUR HANDS TO READ?`

segments.voice: Start with what Sikhs say the book is. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, named the Granth as the Guru after him. So in a gurdwara it isn't handled like a book on a shelf. It rests under a canopy, wrapped in cloth, and the people who come in take off their shoes, cover their heads and bow. Everyone covers their head there, visitors of any faith too. At home the same signs travel with the words: clean hands, a covered head. That sounds like manners. Here's where Guru Nanak turns it. In the Japji he says, in paraphrase: when hands and feet and body are dirty, water washes them clean. When the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name. The water is real. It's also a pointer. The hands get ready first, and they remind the mind it's next. Something to tell a friend tonight: Muslim neighbors know this question from the inside. Before prayer they make wudu, a washing, and the instruction is in the Qur'an itself, in Pickthall's 1930 English: "When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows." Shared ground: clean hands before the holy, because the body helps the heart arrive. And one honest difference. For Muslims, wudu is part of the prayer's own law, with its steps set in the Qur'an. For Sikhs, the washing and the covered head are a way of honoring the Guru, a book treated as a living presence, and Guru Nanak points past the water to the Name.
screen: `THE GRANTH, HONORED AS THE GURU.` · `WATER FOR HANDS, THE NAME FOR THE MIND.` · `WUDU: WASHING BEFORE PRAYER.` · `SHARED GROUND, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `COME READY.`

segments.voice: If there's a sink close by, wash your hands slowly, the way you would before holding something precious; if not, rub your palms together as if they were wet. Cover your head with whatever is clean and near: a scarf, a cloth, a hood. Then sit with your hands open in your lap, and let each breath out rinse off one thing the day left on you.
Coming to the Guru. Approaching the Granth ready: hands washed, head covered, and a mind on its way. The first word of year five.
Your line: come ready. Clean hands and a covered head, with the mind right behind them. Year five, day one.

howItsDone: In a gurdwara, everyone who enters removes their shoes and covers their head before coming before the Guru Granth Sahib; at home, Sikhs commonly wash their hands and cover their heads before reading Gurbani, from a printed book or a screen.

fork.setup: your cousin wants to read a line of Gurbani on her phone during a long train ride. no sink, no scarf in her bag. what does coming to the Guru ask of her?
options: come as ready as she can: settle, cover her head with what she has, and give the words her whole mind.
wait until she's home, since without washing first the reading doesn't count.

fork.reveal: the signs travel with the words, on paper or a screen. and Guru Nanak points past the water: the mind is washed by love of the Name, which a train can't stop.

notes: v3 wisdom day. Question: why wash your hands to read? Sikh answer: coming to the Guru ready, outside and in (Japji 20 turns the outer wash toward the Name).
Japji pauri 20 (Ang 4) is paraphrased: 'bhareeai hath pair tan deh, paanee dhotai utras kheh… bhareeai mat paapaa kai sang, oh dhopai naavai kai rang.' Confirm Ang and paraphrase.
'Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh named the Granth as the Guru after him' is hedged on purpose; no date given.

Gurdwara etiquette (shoes off, head covered, for everyone including visitors) paraphrased from general practice and the Rehat Maryada's gurdwara section; confirm the claim that visitors of any faith cover their heads, and that hand washing before reading is fairly described (the outline's hook line).

Unity thread (Islam neighbor): Qur'an 5:6 quoted from Pickthall 1930: 'O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles.' Only the middle phrase is quoted; confirm exact wording. Shared ground: washing before the holy; honest difference: for Muslims wudu is part of the prayer's law with steps set in the Qur'an; for Sikhs the washing and head covering honor the Guru, and the Japji points past the water to the Name. Confirm a Muslim reader finds this fair and unranked.
The fork's reveal says the signs travel with the words on paper or a screen; Sikhs differ on practice when no water or covering is at hand. Confirm the reveal is fair.
